Python 3 was released in 2008 and Python 2 was not retired until 2020 — twelve years of split ecosystem, two incompatible interpreters, and libraries that had to support both. Perl 6 diverged so far it was renamed Raku and became a different language. AngularJS to Angular 2 was a rewrite, not an upgrade. Swift broke source compatibility annually for its first several years. Every one of those was, technically, the right call — and every one of them cost its community years.

The web made the opposite trade, and it is why the web is the only computing platform where content does not rot. Nothing you publish needs maintenance to keep working. That property is worth more than a clean typeof, and the committee has decided so, consistently, every time the question has come up.

The practical upshot for you, since this is a mastery track and not a history seminar: when you meet something in this language that seems arbitrary, wrong, or redundant with something else, the first hypothesis should be "this is the second attempt, and the first one is still here." That hypothesis is correct startlingly often. It explains var/let/const, ==/===, indexOf/includes, replace/replaceAll, for...in/for...of, isNaN/Number.isNaN, Number/BigInt, Date/Temporal, substr/substring/slice, window/globalThis, scripts/modules, and sloppy/strict. Learning which member of each pair is the modern one is, in practice, a large fraction of learning modern JavaScript.

What this resolves

The assumption in your framing — "previous versions also worked"Section 1: JavaScript has no versions. LANGUAGE="JavaScript1.2" and Mozilla's version=1.8 both failed. There is one version, and every page ever written runs under it. "use strict" works only because it is a no-op string in old engines.
Elaborate the constraint properlySection 2: it is not in the specification. It is enforced by browser vendors refusing to ship breakage, measured with use counters and the HTTP Archive, and anticipated by TC39. The phrase is "don't break the web."
How does the language grow at all, then?Section 3: four hatches — previously-illegal syntax, unclaimed names, parallel APIs, and symbol keys. Plus the ?. lookahead rule as proof that even "free" syntax is constrained by 1995.
What is in the language because of it — the broken partsSection 4: typeof null, ==, ASI, var, let as a legal identifier, global var, with, arguments.callee, octal literals, string sort, array holes, Object.is, and document.all's [[IsHTMLDDA]] slot in the standard
What is in the language because of it — the workaroundsSection 5: a table of seventeen additions that exist only because something could not be fixed, ending with Temporal and why Date is unfixable
Where the language keeps the regretsSection 6: Annex B — HTML comments as JavaScript syntax, __proto__, escape, String.prototype.blink, getYear, substr, and sloppy-mode block function declarations
What could not be doneSection 7: no new reserved words (hence contextual keywords and await being a keyword only in modules), no operator changes, no strict-by-default, no removals, no free prototype methods, no integer type, no Date fix
Has it ever broken?Section 8: SmooshGate (flatten → flat, and contains → includes), parseInt octal in ES5, stable sort in ES2019 — revealing the real rule: specified behaviour is frozen, unspecified behaviour is fixable
What it costs and buysSection 9: TypeScript, ESLint, Babel and bundlers as the cost; a 1996 page running in a 2026 browser as the benefit; and the heuristic that pays off — "this is the second attempt, and the first one is still here"

Three asks and one correction. The catalogue is the answer to "each and everything."

pieces.title: Resolution 4 — Q5: the three declaration forms and the function forms, each one named
pieces.content:
Your complaint is correct and I want to state it back before answering, because it is a good piece of criticism about the shape of an answer, not just its length.

The card asked why does JavaScript have three ways to declare a variable and two ways to write a function, and the answer given was "because backwards compatibility means old mechanisms are never removed — the language grows by layering, not replacing." That sentence is true. It is also the category of the answer rather than the answer. It tells you what kind of explanation applies without ever naming the three ways, the two ways, or a single reason any one of them was added. Resolution 3 then went deep on the constraint itself, which is the same mistake at greater length: it explained the rule and still never listed the things.

This piece is the things. The asks I find in your follow-up:

  1. What are the three ways to declare a variable, concretely. Section 2.
  2. What are the two ways to write a function. Section 4 — and the count is wrong, which Section 3 deals with first.
  3. Why exactly does each one exist — the specific problem each was added to solve, not the general principle. Sections 2 and 4 throughout, and Section 6 gathers the causes in one place.
  4. How are they interconnected? Section 5 — this turns out to be the most useful part, because they are not seven unrelated features but points in one design space with four axes.
  5. Why did each come up when it did? Section 7 — the chronology, and why so much of it lands in a single release in June 2015.

Section 1 — The answer in one screen, before the depth

So that you have it plainly, then the reasoning underneath.

var1995Function-scoped, hoisted and initialised to undefined, silently redeclarable, creates a global-object property at top level. The original, and the source of two famous bugs.
letES2015Block-scoped, hoisted but uninitialised (throws until the declaration runs), not redeclarable, no global-object property, and gets a fresh binding per loop iteration — which is the single feature it was added for.
constES2015Everything let has, plus: must be initialised at the declaration, and the binding can never be reassigned. The value is not frozen.

And the function forms, where the card's "two" is an undercount:

Function declaration1995function f() {} — fully hoisted, name and body
Function expression1995const f = function () {} — created when the expression evaluates
Named function expression1995const f = function inner() {} — inner visible only inside itself
Function constructor1995new Function("a", "return a") — compiles a string, no closure
Arrow functionES2015(a) => a — no this, no arguments, not constructable
Method shorthandES2015{ f() {} } — has a home object, so super works; not constructable
classES2015Still a function underneath, with four behaviours that could not be given to ordinary functions

Plus function*, async function, async () => and async function*, which are modifiers on the above rather than new forms.

Section 2 — The three declaration forms, properly

var — 1995

It is scoped to the enclosing function, not the enclosing block. This is the root property and everything else follows from it.

function f() {
  if (true) {
    var x = 1;
  }
  console.log(x);   // 1 — the block did nothing
}

The mechanism is worth having exactly, because "hoisting" is usually taught as a metaphor and it is not one — it is a real, describable step. When a function is called, before any of its body runs, the engine performs a pass that walks the entire function body, finds every var declaration at any depth of nesting, and creates a binding for each one in the function's variable environment, initialised to undefined. Only then does execution begin. The assignment stays where you wrote it.

So this:

function f() {
  console.log(x);   // undefined — not a ReferenceError
  var x = 5;
  console.log(x);   // 5
}

behaves as though it were written:

function f() {
  var x = undefined;   // created at entry
  console.log(x);
  x = 5;
  console.log(x);
}

Nothing moves. A binding is created early and the assignment is not. The visible consequence is that a variable can be read before its declaration and yields undefined rather than an error, which converts a typo into a silently wrong value — precisely the "never fail loudly" design from Resolution 2, Section 5.

Redeclaration is silently allowed. var x = 1; var x = 2; is legal, and the second declaration is simply ignored (the assignment still runs). This was deliberate for the copy-and-paste audience: a person pasting two scripts from an archive into one page must not get a syntax error because both used var i.

At the top level of a script it creates a property on the global object, and a non-configurable one, so it cannot be deleted:

var a = 1;
console.log(globalThis.a);   // 1
delete globalThis.a;         // false — it stays

The two bugs that made it unfixable and therefore made let necessary.

Bug one — the loop closure. This is the single most reported JavaScript bug of the 2000s:

var fns = [];
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  fns.push(function () { return i; });
}
fns[0]();   // 3
fns[1]();   // 3
fns[2]();   // 3

People expect 0, 1, 2. There is exactly one i, because var is scoped to the function and the loop is not a function. All three closures capture the same binding, and by the time any of them runs the loop has finished and that binding holds 3. Nothing is wrong with closures here; the problem is that the loop did not create a new variable each time round.

From roughly 2000 to 2015 the standard fix was to manufacture a function scope by hand:

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  (function (j) {
    fns.push(function () { return j; });
  })(i);
}

That immediately-invoked function expression exists for one reason: var has no smaller scope than a function, so if you want a smaller scope you must create a function. Hold on to that, because it is also the reason the module pattern looked the way it did, and Section 6 returns to it.

Bug two — the accidental global. Omit var entirely and, in sloppy mode, the assignment creates a property on the global object rather than erroring:

function f() { count = 1; }   // no var — creates globalThis.count
f();
console.log(count);           // 1, from anywhere

Two functions in two different files that both forget var on a variable called i will silently corrupt each other. Strict mode makes this a ReferenceError, which is one of the handful of things strict mode was created to do.

let — ES2015, June 2015

It is scoped to the enclosing block — any pair of braces, plus the head of a for, plus a catch clause.

function f() {
  if (true) { let x = 1; }
  console.log(x);   // ReferenceError: x is not defined
}

The temporal dead zone, and a correction you will need. let is almost always taught as "unlike var, it is not hoisted." That is false, and it is observably false. The binding is created when the block is entered; it is simply left uninitialised, and any access before the declaration executes throws a ReferenceError. The window between block entry and the declaration is the temporal dead zone.

Here is the case that proves the binding must exist from the top of the block:

let x = "outer";
{
  console.log(x);   // ReferenceError — NOT "outer"
  let x = "inner";
}

If the inner let were genuinely absent until its line, the console.log would find the outer x and print "outer". It does not. The inner binding is already shadowing from the opening brace — it just cannot be touched yet. So the accurate statement is: var is hoisted and initialised; let and const are hoisted and uninitialised.

Why have a dead zone at all, rather than just initialising to undefined like var? Two reasons. First, const forces it — a const must be assigned exactly once, at its declaration, so there is no coherent "undefined for now" phase, and having let behave differently from const would have been worse. Second, it turns use-before-declaration from a silently wrong value into a loud error, which is the whole direction of travel of the 2015 additions.

Redeclaration is a SyntaxError — caught at parse time, before the program runs. The copy-paste hazard that var tolerated is now refused.

It does not create a global-object property, and the mechanism behind that is genuinely interesting and explains a confusing observable:

var a = 1;
let b = 2;
globalThis.a;   // 1
globalThis.b;   // undefined — but `b` is perfectly usable

ES2015 gave the global scope two record stores. The global environment record contains an object record, backed by the actual global object (this is where var and function declarations go, which is what keeps window.x working for 1995 code) and a declarative record, which is an ordinary scope with no object behind it (this is where let, const and class go). Lookups check the declarative record first. So let at the top level gives you a real global variable that is invisible on window — a second global namespace, added because the first one could not be cleaned up.

And the feature let was actually added for: a fresh binding per loop iteration.

const fns = [];
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  fns.push(() => i);
}
fns[0]();   // 0
fns[1]();   // 1
fns[2]();   // 2

This deserves emphasis because it is not a consequence of block scoping. Block scoping alone would give you one i for the whole loop head, and you would still get 3, 3, 3. What happens instead is a special rule written into the specification for exactly this case: for a for statement whose head declares with let, the engine creates a new environment for each iteration (the specification operation is literally named CreatePerIterationEnvironment), copies the current value of the loop variable into the new binding, runs the body, and then copies the value back out so the update expression i++ operates on the right thing.

So for (let i ...) is not simpler than for (var i ...) — it is considerably more machinery. That machinery exists because the fifteen-year-old IIFE workaround was so ubiquitous that the committee decided to build it into the loop.

Note also that let was not invented in 2015. Mozilla shipped it as a Firefox-only extension in JavaScript 1.7, with Firefox 2 in 2006, nine years before standardisation. The name comes from let-bindings in Scheme and ML, which is fitting given that JavaScript's semantics came from Scheme in the first place. And per Resolution 3, let could not be made a fully reserved word, which is why var let = 5 is still legal in a sloppy script and the parser needs lookahead to tell a declaration from an assignment.

const — ES2015

The binding is immutable. The value is not. This is the single most misunderstood thing about it:

const a = [1, 2];
a.push(3);      // fine — a is still the same array
a = [4];        // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable

const says the name will never point at a different value. It says nothing about that value's contents. If you want the contents frozen, that is Object.freeze, and it is shallow.

It must be initialised at the declaration — const x; is a SyntaxError — and it is block-scoped and TDZ'd exactly as let is.

The question worth asking is why two new forms rather than one. If block scoping was the fix, one keyword would have delivered it. The answer is that the committee was not only fixing scope; it was choosing a new default. Most bindings in most programs are assigned once and never reassigned, and making that the shorter, more natural thing to write turns "this name is stable" into information the reader gets for free. The style convention that settled afterwards — const unless you must rebind, let when you must, var never — is the intended outcome, not an accident of taste.

One interaction worth knowing: const works in for...of and for...in, because those create a fresh binding per iteration and never reassign it. It does not work in a classic for (;;) loop, because i++ is a reassignment.

for (const item of list) { ... }      // fine
for (const i = 0; i < 3; i++) { ... }  // TypeError on the first i++

And a footnote on "three"

Three is the right headline answer, but if you count every way a name gets bound in a scope, the list is longer: function declarations bind their name, class declarations bind their name (in the declarative record, with a TDZ), function parameters bind, catch (e) binds, and import creates bindings that are genuinely special — immutable and live, so if the exporting module reassigns the value, your imported name sees the change. That last one is a fourth kind of binding semantics, not just a fourth spelling.

Section 3 — "Two ways to write a function" is the wrong number

The card says two. It means function versus =>, and as a headline for Node 0 that is fair. But since you asked for what they actually are and how they interconnect, the honest count is at least seven distinct forms, four of which have existed since 1995. Three of the four originals are usually collapsed into "function expression," and the differences between them are observable and occasionally matter.

Section 4 takes them one at a time; Section 5 shows that they are not seven arbitrary things.

Section 4 — The function forms

1. Function declaration — 1995

function add(a, b) { return a + b; }

Fully hoisted — name and body both. This is a stronger hoisting than var gets. During the same setup pass that gives var bindings the value undefined, function declarations are given their completed function object. So:

console.log(add(1, 2));            // 3 — works
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }

Why the difference? Because a declaration is a complete definition — the engine has everything it needs at setup time. A var whose initialiser is a function expression does not have that; the expression has to be evaluated in sequence.

This is what allows the top-down style where a file reads as "here is the main logic, here are the helpers underneath," which is one of the two reasons function declarations are still the right choice for top-level code in 2026.

2. Function expression — 1995

const add = function (a, b) { return a + b; };

The function object is created when the assignment executes. Before that line runs, the name holds whatever the declaration form gave it. Which produces a distinction worth being precise about:

add(1, 2);
var add = function (a, b) { ... };
// TypeError: add is not a function      — the binding exists, holds undefined

add(1, 2);
let add = function (a, b) { ... };
// ReferenceError: Cannot access 'add' before initialization  — TDZ

Two different errors for the same mistake, and which one you get tells you which declaration form was used. That is the interaction between Section 2 and Section 4, and it is the kind of thing an interviewer asks.

The reason expressions exist at all is that a function has to be a value in this language. You need to pass one to addEventListener, store one in an array, return one from another function. A declaration is a statement and statements do not produce values, so an expression form is not a convenience — it is a requirement of first-class functions.

3. Named function expression — 1995

const fact = function inner(n) {
  return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * inner(n - 1);
};

inner;   // ReferenceError — the name exists only inside the function

The name inner is bound in a scope of its own that wraps the function body and is invisible outside. Two reasons it exists.

Recursion that does not depend on the outer name. If the function recursed via fact, then const g = fact; fact = null; g(5) would break. With the internal name it cannot. Before this pattern was well known, the alternative was arguments.callee — a reference to the currently executing function — and strict mode made arguments.callee throw, which pushed everyone onto named function expressions permanently.

Stack traces. An anonymous function appears in a stack trace as <anonymous>, which is useless during debugging. ES2015 improved this by inferring names from the assignment target in many cases, but the explicit name is still the reliable way.

4. The Function constructor — 1995

const add = new Function("a", "b", "return a + b");
add(1, 2);   // 3

The oldest and least used. It takes strings, compiles them at runtime, and returns a function. The critical property is that it has no closure — the resulting function is compiled in the global scope, so it cannot see any local variable at the point where you called it:

function outer() {
  const secret = 42;
  const f = new Function("return secret");
  return f();     // ReferenceError — `secret` is not visible
}

This is why it survives: it is the mechanism behind runtime template compilation, where a library turns a template string into a fast compiled function, and wants exactly that isolation. It is also why Content Security Policy's unsafe-eval directive blocks it alongside eval — both turn strings into executable code, which is the primary shape of a cross-site scripting payload.

5. Arrow function — ES2015

const add = (a, b) => a + b;
const sq  = n => n * n;
const obj = () => ({ ok: true });   // parens required, or the braces are a block

Everyone learns arrows as shorthand. Brevity was real but secondary. The reason arrows exist is this.

The problem, in the form it appeared in every codebase between 2005 and 2015:

function Counter() {
  this.count = 0;
  setInterval(function () {
    this.count++;             // `this` is not the Counter
  }, 1000);
}

An ordinary function gets a fresh this determined by how it is called, not where it is written — and setInterval calls it as a plain function, so this is the global object in sloppy mode or undefined in strict. The counter never increments, or it throws.

Three workarounds were in wide use, and you will still meet all three in older code:

// 1. capture it in a variable — the most common, ~2005 onward
var self = this;
setInterval(function () { self.count++; }, 1000);

// 2. Function.prototype.bind — ES5, December 2009
setInterval(function () { this.count++; }.bind(this), 1000);

// 3. a `thisArg` parameter, where the API happened to provide one
arr.forEach(function (x) { ... }, this);

An arrow deletes all three, because an arrow has no this of its own at all. It is not that it is bound cleverly at creation; there is simply no this binding in the function's environment, so the identifier this resolves outward through the scope chain exactly like any other variable name. That is the whole mechanism, and it is much simpler than the usual "lexical this" phrasing suggests.

function Counter() {
  this.count = 0;
  setInterval(() => { this.count++; }, 1000);   // works
}

The same absence applies to arguments, super and new.target — all four resolve lexically because the arrow does not create them. And from that, everything else about arrows follows: an arrow has no prototype property and cannot be used with new (TypeError), because constructing requires a fresh this and an arrow has no slot to put one in.

Which yields the rule that matters in practice: an arrow is the wrong tool exactly where dynamic this is the point. Object methods that need the receiver, prototype methods, and DOM event handlers that want this to be the element — Resolution 2, Section 4, on the browser calling your handler as a method of the element — must not be arrows.

const o = {
  n: 1,
  bad:  () => this.n,      // undefined — `this` came from outside `o`
  good() { return this.n; } // 1
};

6. Method shorthand — ES2015

const o = { greet() { return "hi"; } };
// as opposed to
const o = { greet: function () { return "hi"; } };

This looks like pure sugar and is not. A method defined with the shorthand carries an internal slot called [[HomeObject]] — a reference to the object it was defined in — and super is specified in terms of that slot: super.foo() means "look up foo starting at the prototype of my home object." A function assigned as an ordinary property has no home object, so super is a SyntaxError inside it. The shorthand had to be a distinct form because super needed somewhere to anchor.

Shorthand methods are also not constructable — new o.greet() throws — and have no prototype property, because a method is not meant to be a constructor and the empty prototype object on every function was a small permanent waste.

7. class — ES2015

Before 2015, defining a type looked like this, and had done since 1995:

function Point(x, y) {
  this.x = x;
  this.y = y;
}
Point.prototype.norm = function () {
  return Math.sqrt(this.x * this.x + this.y * this.y);
};

function Point3D(x, y, z) {
  Point.call(this, x, y);        // "super" by hand
  this.z = z;
}
Point3D.prototype = Object.create(Point.prototype);
Point3D.prototype.constructor = Point3D;   // easy to forget, and things break

Every library invented its own helper to hide this, incompatibly. class is syntax over exactly the same machinery — a class is a function, typeof Point === "function", and methods still live on Point.prototype. It is emphatically not a second object model.

But it is not only sugar, and the four things it added are precisely the four things that could not be retrofitted to ordinary functions under the constraint from Resolution 3:

  • Class bodies are always strict mode, with no opt-in.
  • The constructor throws if called without new, where Point(1, 2) silently wrote onto the global object.
  • The binding is TDZ'd like let, rather than hoisted like a function declaration.
  • super works, via the home-object mechanism above.

New syntax, previously illegal, therefore free to have better defaults — Hatch 1 from Resolution 3, applied.

Section 5 — How they interconnect: one design space, four axes

This was your fourth ask and it is where the whole thing stops looking like historical clutter. The forms are not seven unrelated features. They are points in a space defined by four independent properties, and each form is a different combination of them.

The axes are: when does the binding become usable (hoisting), does the function get its own this, can it be constructed with new, and which implicit machinery does it carry (arguments, prototype, super).

HoistedOwn thisnewprototypeargumentssuper
Function declarationname + bodyyesyesyesyesno
Function expressionper the declarationyesyesyesyesno
Named function expr.per the declarationyesyesyesyesno
Function constructornoyesyesyesyesno
Method shorthandn/ayesnonoyesyes
Arrowper the declarationnonononolexical
classTDZyesrequiredyesyesyes

Read the bold entries and the design becomes legible. Each 2015 form is the 1995 form with capabilities deliberately removed, because each capability was a source of bugs in the role that form was invented for:

  • An arrow is for a callback. A callback wants the surrounding this, is never constructed, and takes its parameters explicitly. So this, arguments, prototype and constructability are all removed — and removing this is not a restriction, it is the feature.
  • A method is for an object. It wants the receiver, needs super, and is never constructed. So constructability and prototype go, and a home object arrives.
  • A class is for a type. It must be constructed, so calling it without new becomes an error rather than a silent global write.

The 1995 function keyword had to serve all three roles at once, because in 1995 there was one form and it had to do everything. Every 2015 addition is a specialisation of it, with the parts that were wrong for that role taken out.

And the same reading applies on the declaration side. var was one mechanism for all binding; let and const split it by intent — const for "this name is fixed," let for "this name changes" — with block scoping and the TDZ making both fail earlier and louder.

That is the interconnection: 1995 gave one general-purpose tool per job, and 2015 replaced each with a set of specific tools, without being permitted to remove the general-purpose one. Which is what "the language grows by layering" actually means when you cash it out — and is what the original answer should have said.

Section 6 — The specific cause behind each addition

Your third ask, gathered in one place. Every 2015 form exists because of a concrete, nameable failure, not a general desire for elegance.

letThe loop-closure bug (3, 3, 3), the accidental global, and reading a variable before its declaration getting undefined instead of an error. The fifteen-year-old IIFE workaround built into the language.
constAccidental reassignment, and the desire to make "this binding is stable" the default and visible at a glance.
Arrowthis being lost in every callback, and the var self = this / .bind(this) epidemic that resulted. Brevity was the secondary benefit.
Method shorthandsuper needed a home object to anchor to, and object literals were verbose.
classPrototype-and-constructor boilerplate that every library reimplemented differently — plus a chance to get strict mode, new-enforcement and TDZ for free on new syntax.
Named function expression (1995, but it became mandatory later)Strict mode banned arguments.callee, so self-reference needed a legitimate mechanism.

Section 7 — Why so much of this lands on one day in June 2015

Your last ask was why each came up when it did, and the chronology has a shape that is worth seeing, because it explains why modern JavaScript feels like it arrived all at once.

1995var, function declarations, function expressions, named function expressions, the Function constructor
June 1997ECMA-262 1st edition — standardises what exists
December 1999ECMA-262 3rd edition — regular expressions, try/catch, === settled. Then nothing for ten years.
1999–2008ECMAScript 4: an enormous redesign with classes, static types, namespaces, packages. Microsoft and Yahoo opposed it; it split the committee, and it was abandoned in 2008 without shipping. The language stood still for a decade while the web it ran on was transformed by Ajax, jQuery and the arrival of real applications in the browser.
December 2009ES5 — the conservative fallback after ES4 collapsed. Strict mode, Function.prototype.bind, Object.defineProperty, Array.prototype.forEach / map / filter, JSON. Note that bind is a workaround for the this problem, six years before the fix.
June 2015ES2015 — let, const, arrows, classes, method shorthand, template literals, destructuring, default and rest parameters, spread, Promise, Map, Set, Symbol, modules, generators. The single largest release in the language's history.
2016 onwardAnnual releases, deliberately small — ES2016 added two features. The committee moved to a yearly train precisely so that no future release would ever again be a decade-long dam burst.

So the answer to "why did they all come up then" is: they did not come up then; they came due then. Every problem in Section 6 was well known by 2005. The workarounds — IIFEs, var self = this, .bind, hand-rolled inheritance helpers, module patterns — were universal practice for a decade. ES4's failure meant none of it could be fixed, and when a release finally succeeded it carried ten years of accumulated backlog at once. That is also why the duplication is so conspicuous: six replacements arriving together, beside six originals that could never be removed.

Section 8 — What to actually write in 2026

Since the point of knowing this is to make choices without thinking about them:

  • const by default. let only when you genuinely rebind. var never — there is no remaining case where var is the right answer in new code.
  • Function declarations for named top-level functions, because hoisting lets a file read main-logic-first, and because the name is guaranteed in stack traces.
  • Arrows for callbacks and for anything that needs the surrounding this — which is most callbacks.
  • Method shorthand inside objects and classes. Never an arrow as an object method or a prototype method, and never as a DOM event handler where you want this to be the element.
  • class when you are defining a type with a constructor and inheritance; a plain object or a factory function otherwise.
  • new Function essentially never, unless you are writing a template compiler and understand the CSP consequences.

What this resolves

Your complaint — the answer stated the principle and skipped the questionAccepted in the lede. The card gave the category of the answer; Resolution 3 gave the rule at greater length and still never listed the six things. This piece lists them.
What are the three ways?Section 2: var (function-scoped, hoisted-and-initialised, redeclarable, global-object property), let (block-scoped, hoisted-and-uninitialised, per-iteration binding), const (as let, plus one-time initialisation) — with the correction that let is hoisted, proved by the shadowing case
What are the two ways?Sections 3–4: the count is seven, four of them from 1995 — declaration, expression, named expression, Function constructor, arrow, method shorthand, class
Why does each exist?Section 6: a table mapping each form to the specific bug it was created to kill — loop closures, accidental globals, lost this, super's anchor, prototype boilerplate, and strict mode's ban on arguments.callee
How are they interconnected?Section 5: one design space with four axes, and a matrix. Every 2015 form is a 1995 form with capabilities deliberately removed, because 1995 had one general tool per job and 2015 split each into specific ones.
Why did each come up when it did?Section 7: the ES4 collapse in 2008 froze the language from 1999 to 2009, so a decade of known problems and universal workarounds all shipped as fixes in one release in June 2015 — which is why the duplication is so visible
What should I write?Section 8

Five asks, and the one you were right to make: name the things, not the reason there are things.

pieces.title: Resolution 5 — Q6: typeof null, the eight types, and what a type actually is
pieces.content:
This follow-up contains eight asks, and the seventh is the best question in the corpus so far — you caught a real category error, half-apologised for it, and then talked yourself part of the way to the answer. It is not a confusion on your side. It is an ambiguity in the language's own vocabulary, and it is worth a section of its own.

  1. How did typeof null === "object" actually come about? Not "it was a bug" — the actual mechanism. Section 1.
  2. Was it really a bug? Section 2 — the answer is more interesting than yes.
  3. What should it have returned? Section 3, with why the fix was formally proposed and rejected.
  4. Where does object lie among the seven primitives? Section 4 — it does not, and the number you want is eight.
  5. Is your definition of "primitive" right — atomic, not derived, not divisible into sub-parts? Section 5 — instructively wrong, and the real criterion is sharper.
  6. Is null a primitive? Yes. Section 4.
  7. What does typeof return for each of the eight, ideally and actually? Section 6 — there are three anomalies, not one.
  8. Is typeof applied to a value or to a type — and is there a distinction between "type" and "data type"? Sections 7 and 8.

Section 1 — What the bits were actually doing

The cause is not a decision. It is a representation leaking through a switch statement.

In the original engine — Mocha in 1995, then SpiderMonkey from 1996 — a JavaScript value had to be stored in a single machine word, because everything on the stack, in arrays and in object slots had to be uniformly sized and the target machines were 32-bit. But a value can be a number, a string, an object, a boolean or one of the two absences, and the engine has to be able to tell which at runtime, since nothing in the source declares it.

The technique used is called a tagged union, and it is one of the oldest tricks in dynamic-language implementation. You spend a few bits of the word saying what kind of thing this is, and the rest carrying the payload. In this engine the low three bits were the tag:

  31                                    3  2  1  0
 +--------------------------------------+---------+
 |            payload                   |   tag   |
 +--------------------------------------+---------+

 tag 000  →  object    (payload is a pointer to the object)
 tag 001  →  integer   (payload is a 31-bit signed int)
 tag 010  →  double    (payload is a pointer to a double)
 tag 100  →  string    (payload is a pointer to the string)
 tag 110  →  boolean

Why can pointers afford to give up their low bits? Because heap allocations are aligned — an object allocated on an 8-byte boundary has its low three bits zero by construction, so those bits are free storage. The engine masks them off before dereferencing. This is standard practice and it is still what V8 does today in a more elaborate form.

Now the two absences. They are not pointers and not numbers, so they were given fixed special representations. And null was represented as the machine null pointer — a word of all zero bits. That was the natural choice: JavaScript's null was consciously modelled on Java's null, which is a null reference, and the null reference in C and Java is address zero.

Look at what that means for the tag. All zero bits means the low three bits are 000. And 000 is the tag for object.

typeof's implementation was a switch on the tag — read the low bits, return the corresponding string. It had a special case for undefined, because undefined's special representation did not collide with anything. It had no special case for null, because nobody noticed that null already answered "object" without being asked.

// the shape of the original dispatch
switch (TAG_OF(v)) {
  case TAG_OBJECT:   return "object";     // null lands here
  case TAG_INT:
  case TAG_DOUBLE:   return "number";
  case TAG_STRING:   return "string";
  case TAG_BOOLEAN:  return "boolean";
  ...
}

So the answer to "how did this come up in the first place" is: nothing decided it. A storage layout chose it, silently, and the code that should have overridden the layout was never written. The type system of a language used by billions of people has a hole in it because address zero has three zero bits at the bottom.

This is also why the fact is worth carrying beyond the trivia. It is the cleanest example in the language of an implementation detail becoming a specification. Nobody wrote "null shall be of type object" in a design document. An engine did a thing, pages depended on the thing, and the standard was later written to describe what the engine did. That is how a great deal of the web platform came to be, and Resolution 3's Annex B is the same process at scale.

Section 2 — But was it actually a bug? The defensible reading

You assumed it was a bug that got shipped. Almost everyone does, and the card said so too. The honest position is that it is contested, and the case for the defence is worth hearing because it changes what "correct" would even mean.

JavaScript has two absences, and they are not redundant:

undefined   // nobody has put a value here
null        // somebody deliberately put "no object" here

undefined is what you get from an unassigned variable, a missing property, a parameter that was not passed, or a function that returns nothing. It means absence by default. null is never produced by the language on its own; it appears only because a programmer or an API wrote it. It means absence on purpose.

And null was borrowed directly from Java, where it is specifically the null reference — a value of reference type that refers to no object. Under that reading, null is not "no value"; it is "an object reference that currently points at nothing," and answering "object" is arguably the coherent thing to say. It is the same reason null is where you put a value that will later be an object, and the reason APIs return null rather than undefined for "I looked and there was no element there" — document.getElementById returns null, and that is not an accident.

Brendan Eich's own comments over the years have gone both ways: he has called it a bug, and he has also described the object-ish reading as part of the intent, inherited from Java along with null itself. The most accurate summary is: the intent was defensible, the mechanism was accidental, and the result is unusable in practice.

Unusable is the operative word, and it is why the defence loses. Whatever the philosophy, the effect is that the single most common type check in the language is wrong by default:

function isObject(x) {
  return typeof x === "object";     // true for null. Broken.
}

Every codebase in the world has had to write && x !== null after that check, forever, and the ones that forgot produced the most common runtime error in JavaScript's history — Cannot read property 'x' of null.

Section 3 — What it should have returned, and why the fix died

It should have returned "null". That is the answer to your second ask, and it is not merely my opinion — it was a real proposal.

The change typeof null === "null" was drafted during the ECMAScript 4 effort and raised again in the Harmony discussions that led to ES6. It was rejected, and the reasoning is a precise instance of Resolution 3's constraint, so it is worth seeing the actual breakage rather than the general principle.

Code that would keep working:

if (typeof x === "object" && x !== null) { ... }

The defensive form. Unaffected, because it already excluded null explicitly.

Code that would silently change branch:

if (typeof x === "object") {
  handleStructured(x);          // null used to come here
} else {
  handlePrimitive(x);           // and would now come here instead
}

No error, no warning. A value that took one path for twenty years takes the other. That is the worst kind of breakage, because nothing announces it.

Code that would fall off the end:

switch (typeof value) {
  case "string":  ...
  case "number":  ...
  case "boolean": ...
  case "object":  ...     // null was handled here
  default:        throw new Error("unsupported type");   // now null throws
}

Serialisers, form binders, deep-clone helpers and validation libraries are all written this way. A brand-new string in the result set of a thirty-year-old operator means every exhaustive switch over typeof ever written becomes non-exhaustive on the same day.

So the fix has a cost that is unbounded and unmeasurable, and a benefit that is one extra && x !== null per codebase. The committee declined, twice. Object.is, Array.isArray and Object.prototype.toString exist to route around it instead — Hatch 3 from Resolution 3, again.

Section 4 — Where object lies: the number is eight

Your question was "where does object lie in all of this," and the framing has the problem in it. You are looking for object inside the list of seven primitives. It is not inside; it is the eighth entry in a larger list, and the seven are a subset of it.

ECMA-262 defines exactly eight ECMAScript language types:

Undefinedprimitiveone value: undefined
Nullprimitiveone value: null
Booleanprimitivetwo values
Stringprimitivesequences of UTF-16 code units
NumberprimitiveIEEE-754 doubles
BigIntprimitivearbitrary-precision integers (ES2020)
Symbolprimitiveunique, unforgeable property keys (ES2015)
Objectnot primitiveeverything else — arrays, functions, dates, maps, class instances, DOM nodes

So: seven primitives plus Object equals eight types. And yes — null is a primitive, and Null is its own type with exactly one value in it. Same for Undefined. A type with a single member is a perfectly ordinary thing; the two of them exist separately because the language wanted to distinguish default absence from deliberate absence, per Section 2.

Two things that are not on this list and are often assumed to be. Array is not a type — it is an ordinary Object with exotic behaviour on its length property. Function is not a type — a function is an Object with a [[Call]] internal method. That second one matters for Section 6, because typeof reports "function" anyway.

Section 5 — What "primitive" actually means, and why your definition does not survive contact

Your proposed criterion was: a primitive cannot be derived from any other type; it is atomic; it cannot be divided into sub-parts. Your instinct that objects are different because they are collections of key-value pairs is pointing in the right direction, but the criterion itself does not hold, and seeing exactly where it fails is more useful than being handed the right one.

It fails on strings. A string has parts, and you can address them:

const s = "hello";
s.length     // 5
s[0]         // "h"
s.toUpperCase()   // "HELLO"

That is divisible, indexable and has properties. By the atomicity test, a string should not be a primitive. It is one.

The real criterion is two properties, and they are the ones the specification actually turns on:

1. Primitives are immutable. Not the variable — the value. You cannot alter a string; you can only produce a new one.

let s = "hello";
s[0] = "H";        // silently does nothing (TypeError in strict mode)
s;                 // "hello"
s = "Hello";       // this is not mutation — it is rebinding the variable

const o = { a: 1 };
o.a = 2;           // this IS mutation — same object, different contents
o;                 // { a: 2 }

2. Primitives are compared by value; objects are compared by identity. This is the sharper of the two, and it is the one you can test in one line:

"abc" === "abc"     // true  — same value
42 === 42           // true
{} === {}           // false — two separately created objects
[] === []           // false

const a = {};
const b = a;
a === b             // true — the same object, reached by two names

There is no such thing as "two different copies of the string "abc"" that are distinguishable. There are always distinguishable copies of {}. That is the whole distinction, and everything else follows from it — including the one that trips people up constantly, that passing an object to a function lets the function modify your data while passing a string does not.

Now the demonstration that ties your intuition to the truth. If primitives have no properties, how does "hello".length work? Through a mechanism called boxing. When you access a property on a primitive, the engine temporarily wraps it in the corresponding wrapper object (String, Number, Boolean, Symbol, BigInt), reads the property from that object, and then discards the wrapper. Which produces this:

const s = "hello";
s.custom = 123;     // silently accepted (TypeError in strict mode)
s.custom;           // undefined — the box it was written to is gone

const o = new String("hello");   // an explicit box: a real object
o.custom = 123;
o.custom;           // 123 — objects keep what you put on them
typeof o;           // "object", not "string"
o === "hello";      // false — an object is never === a primitive

That is the cleanest experimental proof that a string primitive is not an object, despite appearing to have members. The members belong to a temporary object that exists for the duration of one property access.

So the honest correction: primitives are not "indivisible." They are immutable and compared by value. Your reasoning about objects being collections of key-value pairs is the right observation attached to the wrong rule — the significant thing about an object is not that it has parts, it is that those parts can change while the object stays the same object.

Section 6 — The full typeof table: three anomalies, not one

Your seventh ask was what typeof returns for each type, ideally and actually. Here it is completely. Your predictions were right for six of the seven primitives; the surprises are that there are two more anomalies you did not know about.

ExpressionSpec typetypeof todayCorrect?
typeof undefinedUndefined"undefined"yes
typeof trueBoolean"boolean"yes
typeof 42Number"number"yes
typeof 42nBigInt"bigint"yes
typeof "s"String"string"yes
typeof Symbol()Symbol"symbol"yes
typeof {}Object"object"yes
typeof nullNull"object"no — should be "null"
typeof function () {}Object"function"anomaly, but deliberate
typeof document.allObject"undefined"anomaly, and specified

Anomaly 2 — "function". A function is an Object; there is no Function type in the list in Section 4. But typeof reports "function" anyway, because "can I call this?" is a question people ask constantly and there was no other cheap way to ask it. This one is a deliberate, useful lie, and it is specified. It also means typeof's result set has eight members while the type list has eight different members — they overlap but are not the same list.

Anomaly 3 — document.all. Resolution 3, Section 4 covered this: the [[IsHTMLDDA]] internal slot, written into ECMA-262 so that 1998 browser-sniffing pages keep working. It makes an object report "undefined". Two of the three holes in typeof are therefore backwards-compatibility scars, and the third is a convenience.

And a fourth behaviour that is not an anomaly but is unique in the language. typeof is the only operator that can be applied to a completely undeclared identifier without throwing:

console.log(nonexistent);          // ReferenceError
console.log(typeof nonexistent);   // "undefined" — no error

This is why the classic environment check is written the way it is — before globalThis existed, this was the only safe way to ask whether something was present:

if (typeof window !== "undefined") { /* browser */ }
if (typeof module !== "undefined") { /* CommonJS */ }

One trap, connecting to Resolution 4: this rescue does not apply to the temporal dead zone.

typeof x;        // ReferenceError — x is declared below and is in its TDZ
let x = 1;

Undeclared is forgiven; declared-but-not-yet-initialised is not. That is deliberate — the TDZ exists to catch exactly this mistake, so exempting typeof would have defeated it.

Section 7 — Your sharpest question: is typeof applied to a value or to a type?

You wrote, and I am quoting because it deserves it: "intuitively it feels like typeof is primarily intended to check the type of a particular value or variable… but here typeof was applied to an actual primitive type, a type itself."

You are right that something is off, and the fault is in the language's naming, not in your thinking. Here is the resolution.

typeof is an operator on values. Always. It evaluates its operand to a value and reports that value's type. It has no ability to take a type as input, because types are not values in JavaScript. There is no expression anywhere in the language that evaluates to "the Number type." You cannot store a type in a variable, pass it to a function, or compare two types.

So why did typeof null feel like you were applying it to a type? Because of a genuine collision in the vocabulary:

nulla literal — an expression that evaluates to the single value of the Null type
Nulla type name — used only in the specification, never in your code

The value and the type are spelled almost identically, so typeof null reads as though you are asking about the type. You are not. You are asking about a value that happens to be the only inhabitant of its type. It is exactly the same as typeof true — true is a value, Boolean is its type, and nobody gets confused there because the two are spelled differently.

The clinching demonstration. Try applying typeof to the things you listed as types:

typeof number      // "undefined"  — `number` is not an identifier in JS at all
typeof string      // "undefined"
typeof boolean     // "undefined"

Not an error — because of the undeclared-identifier rule in Section 6 — but "undefined", which tells you plainly that number is simply not a thing in JavaScript. It is a name that does not exist. Contrast:

typeof Number      // "function"  — the constructor, which IS a real value
typeof Object      // "function"
typeof Symbol      // "function"

Those are values: the wrapper constructors from Section 5. They are objects that exist at runtime, not types.

And here is where your confusion almost certainly came from, given what else you are studying. In TypeScript, number, string and boolean are real names — they live in a second, parallel namespace of types that exists only at compile time:

let x: number = 5;              // `number` is a type name — TypeScript only

type T = typeof x;              // TypeScript's `typeof`, at the type level → number

console.log(typeof x);          // JavaScript's `typeof`, at runtime → "number"

Those two typeofs are different operators that share a spelling. TypeScript's takes a variable and yields a type; JavaScript's takes a value and yields a string. And TypeScript's entire type layer is erased before the code runs — the compiled output contains no trace of : number, and at runtime there is nothing to inspect but the tag bits from Section 1. So if you have been moving between the two topics, you have been seeing type names treated as first-class in one language and not existing at all in the other. Your instinct that you had crossed a category line was correct; you had, and the line is between the two languages.

Section 8 — Is there a distinction between "type" and "data type"?

Your last ask. You hypothesised that "type" might be a superset — carrying information about which operations are valid — while "data type" says only what kind of data something is.

The direct answer: no, those two terms are used interchangeably in practice. "Data type" is the older, more textbook-flavoured spelling; "type" is what specifications and type theory use. ECMA-262 says "type." There is no technical distinction between the words.

But your intuition is tracking a real distinction, and it is an important one — you attached it to the wrong pair of words. There are two genuine distinctions here, and both are worth having.

Distinction one: a type really is "a set of values plus the operations on them." This is the formal definition from type theory, and it is precisely what you reached for. A type is not only a label on data; it is the label together with what you are allowed to do with it. And JavaScript has a beautiful demonstration of why the operations are part of the identity — Number and BigInt:

1 + 1        // 2
1n + 1n      // 2n
1n + 1       // TypeError: Cannot mix BigInt and other types

Both hold integers. Both are "numbers" in any ordinary sense. They are separate types because their operations are separate — one is IEEE-754 with rounding, one is exact and unbounded — and the language refuses to mix them precisely so the difference cannot be papered over silently. If a type were only a description of the data, BigInt would not need to exist.

Distinction two — and this is the superset/subset relationship you were feeling: runtime type versus static type.

In JavaScript, values have types; variables do not.

let x = 5;        // the value 5 has type Number
x = "hello";      // now the value "hello" has type String
                  // `x` never had a type at any point

x is a name bound to a slot. The type lives in the value, physically, as the tag bits from Section 1. This is what "dynamically typed" means, and it is why typeof has to be a runtime operator that inspects a value — there is nowhere else the information could be.

In a statically typed language the arrangement is the reverse. In C:

int x = 5;
x = "hello";      // compile error — caught before the program runs

Here the variable has the type, the compiler knows it, and — this is the part that surprises people — the value at runtime may carry no type information at all. An int in memory is thirty-two bits with nothing marking them as an integer. The type existed at compile time, did its job of checking your operations, and then evaporated. There is no typeof in C because at runtime there is nothing left to ask.

So the real hierarchy you were sensing is:

Static typeA compile-time claim about what a variable or expression may hold, and which operations are legal on it. Checked before running. Usually erased afterwards. This is the "superset" — it carries the operation rules.
Runtime type / tagA property carried by an actual value while the program runs, saying what kind of thing it is. This is what typeof reads. It is the narrower notion — a label, not a rulebook.

And that is exactly the relationship between TypeScript and JavaScript. TypeScript adds the first layer; JavaScript has only the second; the first is deleted at build time and the second is all that survives. Which means the sentence worth memorising is:

TypeScript's types are claims about your program. JavaScript's types are facts about your values.

Section 9 — What to actually use for type checks

Since typeof has three holes in it:

// primitives — typeof is correct and fast
typeof x === "string"
typeof x === "number"
typeof x === "function"

// null — there is exactly one right way
x === null

// "is this a non-null object?" — the check every codebase needs
x !== null && (typeof x === "object" || typeof x === "function")

// arrays — typeof says "object", which is useless
Array.isArray(x)

// the general-purpose classifier
Object.prototype.toString.call(x)

That last one is worth seeing, because it delivers the punchline of this whole piece:

Object.prototype.toString.call(null)        // "[object Null]"
Object.prototype.toString.call(undefined)   // "[object Undefined]"
Object.prototype.toString.call([])          // "[object Array]"
Object.prototype.toString.call(new Date())  // "[object Date]"
Object.prototype.toString.call(/x/)         // "[object RegExp]"

The engine knows perfectly well that null is Null. It says so, right there, in a different operator. It is only typeof that lies, because only typeof is dispatching on the tag bits. And note that ES5, in December 2009, had to explicitly specify that null gives "[object Null]" and undefined gives "[object Undefined]" — under ES3 those cases were implementation-dependent and engines disagreed. Which is the rule from Resolution 3, Section 8 in action: unspecified behaviour could be fixed, specified behaviour could not. toString was unspecified for these, so it was repaired. typeof was specified, so it never can be.

What this resolves

How did typeof null === "object" come about?Section 1: a tagged-union value representation with the object tag at 000, and null stored as the machine null pointer — all zero bits. typeof switched on the tag and there was no case for null. An implementation detail became a specification.
Was it a bug?Section 2: contested. null came from Java's null reference, so "object" has a defensible reading. The intent was defensible, the mechanism accidental, the result unusable.
What should it have returned?Section 3: "null". Formally proposed for ES4 and again for ES6, rejected both times — with the three concrete breakage shapes shown.
Where does object lie among the primitives?Section 4: it does not. There are eight language types — seven primitives plus Object. Array and Function are not types.
Is null a primitive?Section 4: yes, and Null is a type with exactly one value in it.
Is "atomic / indivisible" the right definition of primitive?Section 5: no — strings have parts. The real criteria are immutable and compared by value. Demonstrated with boxing: s.custom = 123 then s.custom is undefined, because the wrapper is discarded.
typeof for all eight, ideal vs actualSection 6: full table. Your predictions were right; there are three anomalies, not one — null, function (deliberate), and document.all (specified web-compat). Plus the undeclared-identifier rule, and why the TDZ is exempt from it.
Is typeof applied to a value or a type?Section 7: always a value. Types are not values in JavaScript — typeof number returns "undefined" because number is not an identifier. Your sense of a category error was correct: the line you crossed is the one between JavaScript and TypeScript, where number is a real name in a compile-time-only namespace.
Type versus data typeSection 8: the two words mean the same thing, but your intuition was tracking two real distinctions — a type is a set of values plus its operations (why BigInt had to be separate from Number), and static types are claims about variables while runtime tags are facts about values
What to use insteadSection 9 — including Object.prototype.toString.call(null) returning "[object Null]", which proves the engine knew all along and only typeof lies

Eight asks. The seventh was the best one, and it was right.

pieces.title: Resolution 6 — Q7: the sandbox, the single thread, and why the fourth constraint does not belong
pieces.content:
Resolution 1 answered part of this follow-up — the parser-blocking mechanism, and the correction that "never break old pages" does not belong with the other three. But it answered a different question from the one you actually asked about freezing. You asked for the history: was there a real incident, was it an architectural problem in the browsers themselves, and how could a script physically interfere with the drawing of a page. Resolution 1 explained why blocking is mandatory and explicitly said "it is not that anyone feared scripts freezing pages," which answers the mechanism and skips the history. The history is real and it is Sections 4 through 6 here.

The asks I find:

  1. Check my reading — untrusted server, unknown intent, so make the browser a secure environment with no direct access to the machine. Is that right? Section 1, and it is largely right, with the actual 1995 threat model that you did not name.
  2. Is that what sandboxing is, and did the concept come from browsers? Section 2 — the concept runs the other way round.
  3. Are "never access files" and "never crash the machine" the same constraint? You said they were, then corrected yourself mid-sentence. Section 3 — your correction was right.
  4. The actual history of "never freeze the page" — were there incidents? Section 4.
  5. Was it an architectural issue of the browser? How could a script interfere with the pipeline that displays content? Section 5 — yes, and this is the deepest answer in the piece.
  6. The two files again — "I'm not really sure how that actually used to work back then." Answered in full in Resolution 2, Section 1: <SCRIPT SRC>, absent from Navigator 2.0, added in Navigator 3.0 in August 1996.
  7. How does "never break old pages" relate to untrusted code at all? Section 7 — it does not, you were right, and the card is wrong.

Section 1 — Your security reading, checked

Your account is: the user clicks a link, the server is a stranger, the stranger's intentions are unknown, we cannot control what code they ship, so the defence has to be at the receiving end — make the browser an environment where that code cannot reach the machine. That is correct, and it is the right instinct in a way worth naming: you located the defence at the correct layer. The alternative approaches — trusting the server, checking code before running it, asking the user to approve — were all tried elsewhere and all failed, and it is worth seeing why, because it makes the browser model look less obvious and more earned.

Trusting the server is what installed software does, and the web's whole premise is that you visit sites you have never heard of, on one click, with no decision. Checking the code first is undecidable in general — you cannot determine by inspection whether a program will do something bad. Asking the user is what ActiveX did: Internet Explorer showed a dialog saying this control is signed by so-and-so, do you want to run it, and users clicked yes, and ActiveX became one of the most productive malware vectors of the late 1990s. A signature tells you who wrote the code, not whether it is safe, and users cannot evaluate the difference.

So the browser's answer is the only one left: run the code, but in an environment where the dangerous operations do not exist. Which is what Resolution 1 called security by absence — no file API, no process API, no arbitrary network access, so there is nothing to abuse.

But there is a threat you did not name, and it is the one that actually mattered. Your model is about the code reaching your machine. The far more important threat, from 1995 to today, is the code reaching other websites through your browser.

Think about what the browser is holding while you are on a stranger's page. Your session cookie for your bank. Your logged-in state at your email provider. Your identity everywhere you have signed in. The browser attaches those cookies automatically to requests. So if the stranger's script could simply read the contents of another page, or issue a request to your bank and read the response, it would not need to touch your filesystem at all — your files are not where the valuable things are.

The defence is the same-origin policy, introduced by Netscape in Navigator 2.0, 1995 — the same release that introduced JavaScript, and not a coincidence. It is the single most important security rule on the web, and the rule is small:

Script from one origin may not read data from a different origin. An origin is the triple (scheme, host, port), and all three must match exactly.

https://example.com/a     and  https://example.com/b     — same origin
https://example.com       and  http://example.com        — different (scheme)
https://example.com       and  https://api.example.com   — different (host)
https://example.com       and  https://example.com:8443  — different (port)

So a script on evil.com can put your bank in an <iframe> — but cannot read a single character out of it. It can send a request to your bank, and the cookies will even be attached, but it cannot read the response. Note the asymmetry carefully: the policy restricts reading, not sending. That gap is exactly the CSRF vulnerability class, which is why servers need anti-CSRF tokens and why SameSite cookies were eventually introduced — a hole in the 1995 model still being patched thirty years later.

Two things follow that are worth having, because they explain APIs you use constantly.

CORS exists because the same-origin policy is too strict for legitimate use. Access-Control-Allow-Origin is the server saying "I consent to being read by this other origin." Every CORS error you have ever debugged is the 1995 policy doing its job and the server not having opted out of it.

document.domain was the original escape hatch — two pages could each set it to a shared parent domain and become same-origin. It was a bad idea, widely exploited, and browsers have now disabled it by default. Another 1995 convenience walked back.

Section 2 — Where "sandbox" came from: your guess runs backwards

You wrote that maybe the concept of a sandboxed, isolated environment "came from this thing only, especially the browsers." It is the reverse. The concept predates the browser, and the browser's first explicit sandbox was not JavaScript's.

The idea of confining untrusted code so it cannot harm its host is decades older — it runs through operating-system protection rings, capability systems, and chroot in Unix (1979). The term became standard in the security literature with Wahbe, Lucco, Anderson and Graham's "Efficient Software-Based Fault Isolation" (1993), which described confining an untrusted module inside a fault domain within a single address space — sandboxing without the cost of separate processes.

What made the word mainstream was Java's applet sandbox, 1995 — the same year, from Sun, arriving in Navigator 2.0 alongside JavaScript. Java's was a real, designed, explicit sandbox: a SecurityManager object consulted before every sensitive operation, a bytecode verifier that checked the code before running it, and a documented list of what an applet could and could not do. It was engineering, and the word "sandbox" entered the popular vocabulary through it.

JavaScript's was nothing like that. It had no security manager, no verifier, no policy object. Per Resolution 1: it was enforced by absence. There was no function that opened a file, so no file could be opened. The only actual policy was the same-origin rule from Section 1. It was a sandbox in the sense that a room with no doors is a locked room.

And the irony worth carrying: the designed sandbox failed and the accidental one held. Java applets accumulated a long history of sandbox escapes — verifier bugs, security-manager bypasses — and by 2013 browsers were disabling the Java plugin by default. The applet is gone. JavaScript's model, which had almost no security architecture at all, survived, because a capability you never implemented cannot have a bug in it.

Now your tab-isolation intuition, which Resolution 1 corrected on dates and which is worth building out properly, because it is more layered than either of us said. Browser isolation arrived in four distinct stages over twenty-three years:

1995Same-origin policy. A logical rule inside one process. Nothing is isolated by the operating system; the engine simply refuses cross-origin reads.
~2001–2003Tabs arrive (Opera, the Mozilla suite, then Firefox). Purely a user-interface feature. Every tab is still in one process, sharing one heap. One tab crashing takes the whole browser with it, which is precisely how browsers behaved.
2008Process-per-tab, with Chrome. Now the operating system enforces it: a crash kills one tab, and a compromised renderer is confined by OS-level sandboxing to a process with almost no privileges — it cannot open files or make syscalls directly, and must ask a privileged browser process for everything.
2018+Site isolation. After Spectre and Meltdown showed that any code sharing an address space could read that whole address space through CPU cache timing, process-per-tab was no longer enough — a cross-origin iframe in your tab was in your process. Site isolation puts each site in its own process, so a hardware side channel cannot reach another site's data because that data is not in the same address space at all.

So your instinct that isolation is the point was right, and the thing to correct is the timeline and the direction of travel: the isolation was not there in 1995 and has been progressively hardened ever since, most recently because a CPU bug invalidated the previous model.

Section 3 — "Never access files" and "never crash the machine" are not one constraint

You wrote that these are "one and the same thing," then immediately corrected yourself — "not one and the same thing exactly." Your correction was right, and the distinction is worth making sharp, because they are different threats with different defences and different histories.

Never read or write the user's filesA confidentiality and integrity threat. The attacker wants to take something or change something. Defence: the capability does not exist — no file API in the language, and later, a file API that only works on files the user explicitly picked in a system dialog.
Never crash or hang the machineAn availability threat. The attacker takes nothing; they deny you the use of your own computer. Defence: resource limits, watchdogs, and process isolation — entirely different machinery.

They are separated in practice too. A page that hangs your browser has stolen nothing, and yet it is a real attack that people run for money: the "browser locker" tech-support scam is a page that makes the browser unusable — historically with an infinite loop, or an unending chain of modal dialogs — while displaying a phone number to call. It is pure denial of availability, it steals nothing directly, and browsers had to add specific defences against it (the "prevent this page from creating additional dialogs" checkbox exists because of exactly this).

And the histories are opposite. The file constraint has held since 1995 and has never seriously been breached at the language level; the modern File System Access API is gated behind an explicit user gesture and a system file picker, which keeps the property that the page cannot choose what it touches. The availability constraint has never been fully solved, is not solved today, and Section 4 is why.

Section 4 — The freezing constraint: the history you asked for

Here is the honest sequence, and it starts with a correction to the card.

"Never freeze the page's rendering" was not a design constraint anyone wrote down in 1995. The card lists it alongside the others as though it were a requirement handed to Eich. It was not. It is a property that turned out to be unachievable, and the history is a history of browsers building defences after the fact rather than a history of a rule being obeyed.

Resolution 1 gave the first half: document.write injects into the tokenizer's input stream, so the parser cannot proceed past a <script> without running it. That is why script blocks parsing. But that is only the loading-time story, and your question is broader — you asked how a script could interfere with the display of content generally. The general answer is Section 5. First, the incidents you asked about.

The incident is not one event. It is a permanent condition, and the evidence is that every browser built a defence for it.

Write this in any browser, from 1995 to right now:

while (true) {}

The tab stops. Not slows — stops. It does not repaint, does not scroll, does not respond to clicks, and the close button on the tab may not respond either. This has been true for thirty-one years and it is true in the browser you are reading this in.

Because there is no way to prevent it, browsers instead built watchdogs, and the details are period-accurate evidence of how big a problem it was:

Internet Explorer counted statements. The engine incremented a counter per script statement executed and, when it passed a threshold — the default was 5,000,000 statements, configurable through a registry value named MaxScriptStatements — it stopped and showed the dialog: "A script on this page is causing Internet Explorer to run slowly. If it continues to run, your computer may become unresponsive. Do you want to abort the script?" A statement count rather than a timer is a revealing choice: it made the limit reproducible across machine speeds, and it also meant a script doing five million trivial statements was punished the same as one doing five million expensive ones. IE9 later moved to a time-based limit.

Firefox used, and still has, a preference called dom.max_script_run_time — historically ten seconds — after which it offers to stop the script.

Chrome took a different route, which follows directly from the 2008 process-per-tab architecture in Section 2: rather than interrupting the script, it lets the tab hang and offers to kill the whole renderer process — the "Page unresponsive: wait / exit page" dialog. Chrome could afford that answer because killing one tab no longer killed the browser.

Three different vendors, three different mechanisms, all built for the same purpose. That is your incident: not a famous single event, but a failure mode common enough that every browser shipped a user-facing dialog for it, and those dialogs became one of the most recognisable pieces of 2000s computing.

The second and more common form of the problem is not the infinite loop but the merely slow script, and it is the one that shapes web development today. A script that takes 400 milliseconds does not trigger any dialog. It simply makes the page stop responding for 400 milliseconds — scrolling stutters, a button press does nothing, typing lags. That is jank, and it is the single most common performance complaint about web applications. Section 5 is why it happens.

Section 5 — Yes, it is architectural. One thread, and run-to-completion

You asked directly: "was it some architectural issue of the browser itself, as in how they actually carried out all of the required operations?" Yes. Two facts, and everything follows from them.

Fact one: script and rendering share one thread.

A browser renders a page through a pipeline:

JavaScript  →  Style  →  Layout  →  Paint  →  Composite
(run code)     (which   (where     (draw     (assemble
               CSS       does each  pixels)   layers on
               applies)  box go)              the GPU)

Everything from JavaScript through Paint runs on one thread — the main thread — per page. Not per browser: Chrome's process-per-tab isolates tabs from each other, but inside one tab there is still a single main thread doing all of it. So your intuition about tab isolation, which was correct as far as it went, has a precise limit worth stating:

Tabs are isolated from each other. A script is not isolated from its own page's rendering. It is the same thread that does the rendering.

Which answers your question of how a script could interfere with the display of content. It does not interfere with rendering. It occupies the thread that rendering would run on. While your function is executing, style, layout and paint are not merely delayed — they cannot be scheduled at all, because the one worker that performs them is inside your function.

Fact two: JavaScript runs to completion and cannot be preempted.

The browser's event loop is, in outline:

forever:
    take one task from the queue      (a script, an event handler, a timer callback)
    run it to completion              ← no interruption is possible here
    drain the microtask queue         (promise callbacks)
    if it is time to draw a frame:
        run requestAnimationFrame callbacks
        style → layout → paint → composite

The critical property is on the highlighted line. Once a task starts, nothing can stop it. The browser cannot pause your function halfway to repaint and resume it afterwards. There is no preemptive scheduler for JavaScript.

And now the thing that makes this genuinely interesting rather than merely a limitation. Run-to-completion is not a defect. It is a guarantee, and it is one of the most valuable properties the language has.

Because no other JavaScript can run while your function is running, you can do this and be certain it is safe:

total = total - amount;
count = count + 1;
// nothing can observe the state between these two lines

In a preemptively threaded language that is a race condition and needs a lock. In JavaScript it is simply correct. There are no mutexes in JavaScript, no synchronized, no deadlocks, no torn reads — because nothing can interrupt you. Every callback, every event handler, every promise continuation runs alone.

So the two properties are one property seen from two sides:

"Nothing can interrupt my code" and "my slow code freezes the page" are the same sentence.

You cannot have the first without the second. The language traded preemption for simplicity, and got a concurrency model an untrained programmer can use correctly, at the cost of a page that stops whenever any script is slow. That trade is the origin of the entire second half of this landscape — the event loop, callbacks, promises, async/await at Node 9 all exist to let you express "wait for something" without occupying the thread while you wait. Every asynchronous mechanism in JavaScript is a workaround for the fact that blocking is not allowed.

One quantitative addition, because it explains modern performance work. A display refreshing at 60 Hz gives you 16.7 milliseconds per frame for everything: your script, style, layout, paint. Exceed it and a frame is dropped, which the eye reads as stutter. The Long Tasks API defines a "long task" as anything occupying the main thread for over 50 ms, and Interaction to Next Paint (INP) — which became a Core Web Vital in March 2024, replacing First Input Delay — measures precisely the gap between a user interacting and the screen updating. That metric exists because of the architecture in this section. It is the 1995 single-threaded design, still being measured.

Section 6 — What was done about it, 2009 to now

Since the constraint could not be met, the platform spent twenty years building ways around it. Each one is a different answer to "get the work off the main thread, or give the thread back."
